readings.c2s1:
¶
'''II.''' ''a.'' Recently weaned.
{{smaller block|<poem>As killing as the canker to the rose,
Or taint-worm to the ''weanling'' herds.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 46.}}}}

'''weapon''' (wep′ọn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wepen'', ''weppon'', ''wapen'', ''wopen'', < AS. ''wǣpen'', ''wǣpn'', a weapon, shield, sword, = OS. ''wāpan'', sword, = OFries. ''wēpin'', ''wēpen'', ''wēpn'' = D. ''wapen'' = MLG. LG. ''wapen'' = OHG. ''waffan'', ''wafan'', MHG. ''wappen'', ''wafen'', G. ''waffen'', weapon (cf. G. ''wappen'', scutcheon, coat of arms, < D. or LG.), = Icel. ''vāpn'' = Sw. ''vapen'' = Dan. ''vaaben'' = Goth. pl. ''wēpna'', weapon.] '''1.''' Any instrument of offense; anything used, or designed to be used, in attacking an enemy, as a sword, a dagger, a club, a rifle, or a cannon.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ector faght in the fild felle of his Enmys.
Polexenas, a pert Duke, that the prinse met,
He dang to the dethe with his derfe ''weppon''.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7740.}}
<poem>Before they durst
Embrace, they were by several servants search’d,
As doubting conceal’d ''weapons''.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and others''), Bloody Brother, i. 1.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' Any object, particular, or instrumentality that may be of service in a contest or struggle, or in resisting adverse circumstances, whether for offense or defense; anything that may figuratively be classed among arms.
{{smaller block|The ''weapons'' of our warfare are not carnal. 2 Cor. x. 4.
<poem>All his mind is bent to holiness; . . .
His ''weapons'', holy saws of sacred writ.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., i. 3. 61.}}}}

¶
'''weaponry†''' (wep′on-ri), ''n.'' [< ''weapon'' + ''-ry'' (see ''-ery'').] Weapons in general. [Rare.]

'''weapon-salve†''' (wep′ọn-säv), ''n.'' A salve which was supposed to cure a wound by being applied to the weapon that made it. {{smaller|According to Sir Kenelm Digby, the salve produces sympathy between the wound and the weapon; he cites several instances to prove that “as the sword is treated the wound inflicted by it feels. Thus, if the instrument is kept wet, the wound will feel cool; if held to the fire, it will feel hot,” etc. This superstition is referred to in the following lines:}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She has ta’en the broken lance,
And washed it from the clotted gore,
And salved the splinter o’er and o’er.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iii. 23.}}}}

'''weapon-smith''' (wep′ọn-smith), ''n.'' One who makes weapons of war; an armorer. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It is unavoidable that the first mechanics — beyond the heroical ''weapon-smith'' on the one hand, and on the other the poor professors of such rude arts as the homestead cannot do without — . . . should be those who have no land.
{{right|''J. M. Kemble'', Saxons in England, ii. 7.}}}}

'''wear<sup>1</sup>''' (wãr), ''v.''; pret. ''wore'', pp. ''worn'', ppr. ''wearing''. [< ME. ''weren'', ''werien'' (pret. ''werede'', pp. ''wered''), < AS. ''werian'' (pret. ''werode'', pp. ''werod''), wear, = OHG. ''werjan'', ''werjen'', clothe, = Icel. ''verja'', clothe, wrap, inclose, mount, also lay out, spend, = Goth. ''wasjan'' (pl. ''wasida''), clothe (the Goth. form showing interchange of ''r'' and ''s'': see ''rhotacism''), < √ ''was'', clothe, in L. ''vestis'', clothing, ''vestire'', clothe, Gr. ἐσθής, clothing: see ''vest''. The pret. ''wore'' (formerly also ''ware''), with the pp. ''worn'', is due to conformity with orig. strong preterits like ''bore'' < ''bear'', ''swore'' < ''swear'', ''tore'' < ''tear'', etc. (pp. ''born'', ''sworn'', ''torn'', etc.), the ME. pret. being weak, ''wered'', mod. E. *''weared''.]

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wealthful|6859|wear}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''wealthful†''' (welth′fůl), ''a.''   [< ''wealth'' + ''-ful.'']   Full of wealth or happiness; prosperous.   ''Sir T. More.''

'''wealthfully†''' (welth′fůl-i), ''adv.'' In prosperity or happiness; prosperously.
{{smaller block|To lead thy life ''wealthfully.''
{{right|''Vives,'' Instruction of a Christian Woman, ii. 2.}}}}

'''wealthily''' (wel′thi-li), ''adv.'' In a wealthy manner; in the midst of wealth; richly.
{{smaller block|<poem>I come to wive it ''wealthily'' in Padua;
If ''wealthily,'' then happily in Padua.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' T. of the S., i. 2. 75.}}}}

'''wealthiness''' (wel′thi-nes), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''welthiness;'' < ''wealthy'' + ''-ness.'']   The state of being wealthy; wealth.
{{smaller block|The Fosterer vp of shoting is Labour, companion of vertue, the maynteyner of honestie, the encreaser of health and ''welthinesse.''
{{right|''Ascham,'' Toxophilus (ed. Arber), p. 52.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is a more sound ''wealthinesse'' for a man to esteeme him selfe wise than to presume to be of great wealth; for with wisdom they obteine to haue, but with hauing they come to lose themselues.
{{right|''Guevara,'' Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 191.}}}}

'''wealthy''' (wel′thi), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. ''welthy, welthie;'' < ''wealth'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Having wealth; rich; having large possessions; opulent; affluent.
{{smaller block|Married to a ''wealthy'' widow.
{{right|''Shak.,'' T. of the S., iv. 2. 37.}}}}
'''2.''' Rich in any sense, as in beauty, ornament, endowments, etc.; enriched.
{{smaller block|Thou broughtest us out into a ''wealthy'' place.
{{right|Ps. lxvi. 12.}}}}

{{smaller block|Her dowry ''wealthy''. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 5. 65.}}}}

<poem>’Twas a tough Task, believe it, thus to tame
A wild and ''wealthy'' Language, and to frame
Grammatic Toils to curb her, so that she
Now speaks by Rules, and sings by Prosody.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 26.}}}}

<poem>Revealings deep and clear are thine
Of ''wealthy'' smiles.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Madeline.}}}}

'''3.''' Well-fed; in good condition.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] ='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|Moneyed, well off, well to do.}}

'''weam†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''wem.''

'''wean''' (wēn), ''v. t.''   [Formerly also ''wain''; < ME. ''wenen'', < AS. ''wenian'' (''ge-wenian'', accustom, also wean, ''ā-wenian'', wean) = D. ''wennen'', accustom (''ge-wennen'', accustom, inure, ''af-wennen'', wean), = OHG. ''wenjan'', ''wennen'', ''wenen'', MHG. ''wenen'', accustom (OHG. MHG. ''ge-wenen'', G. ''ge-wöhnen'', accustom, OHG. ''int-wennan'', MHG. ''entwenen'', G. ''entwöhnen'', disaccustom, wean), = Icel. ''venja'' = Sw. ''vänja'' = Dan. ''vænne'' = Goth. ''wanjan'', accustom; connected with OHG. ''giwona'', MHG. ''gewona'' = Icel. ''vani'' = Sw. ''vana'' = Dan. ''vane'', custom, from an adj. seen in OHG. ''giwon'', MHG. ''gewon'', G. *''gewohn'' (in ''gewohnheit'', custom), ''gewohnt'' = Icel. ''vanr'' = Sw. ''van'', ''vand'' = Dan. ''vant'', accustomed: connected with ''wone''<sup>1</sup>, ''wont'', q. v.]   '''1.''' To accustom (a child or young animal) to nourishment or food other than its mother’s milk; disaccustom to the mother’s breast: as, to ''wean'' a child.

{{smaller block|And the child grew, and was ''weaned''. {{right|Gen. xxi. 8.}}}}

{{smaller block|For the widowes and Orphans, for the sucking and ''wained''. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 198.}}}}

'''2.''' To detach or alienate, as the affections, from any object of desire; reconcile to the want or loss of something; disengage from any habit, former pursuit, or enjoyment: as, to ''wean'' the heart from temporal enjoyments.
{{smaller block|Riper years will ''wean'' him from such toys.
{{right|''Marlowe'', Edward II., i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I will restore to thee
The people’s hearts, and ''wean'' them from themselves.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., i. 1. 211.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Could I, by any practice, ''wean'' the boy
From one vain course of study he affects.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|My Father would willingly have ''weaned'' me from my fondness of my too indulgent Grandmother, intending to have me placed at Eaton. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 21, 1632.}}}}

'''Weaning brash.''' See ''brash''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wean''' (wēn), ''n.''   [< ''wean'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' An infant; a weanling. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|<poem>What gars this din of mirk and balefull harme,
Where euery ''weane'' is all betaint with bloud?</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', James IV., i. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' A child; a boy or girl of tender age. [Scotch.]

'''weanel†, weanell†''' (wē′nel), ''n.''   [< ''wean'' + dim. ''-el.'']   A weanling; an animal newly weaned.
{{smaller block|A Lambe, or a Kidde, or a ''weanell'' wast.
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., September.}}}}

'''weanling''' (wēn′ling), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< ''wean'' + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' A child or young animal newly weaned.
{{smaller block|As a ''weanling'' from the mother, I will bewail my woe ful state.
{{right|''J. Careless'', in Bradford’s Works (Parker Soc.), II. 357.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Recently weaned.
{{smaller block|<poem>As killing as the canker to the rose,
Or taint-worm to the ''weanling'' herds.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 46.}}}}

''wēpin'', ''wēpen'', ''wēpn'' = D. ''wapen'' = MLG. LG. ''wapen'' = OHG. ''waffan'', ''wafan'', MHG. ''wappen'', ''wafen'', G. ''waffen'', weapon (cf. G. ''wappen'', scutcheon, coat of arms, < D. or LG.), = Icel. ''vāpn'' = Sw. ''vapen'' = Dan. ''vaaben'' = Goth. pl. ''wēpna'', weapon.]   '''1.''' Any instrument of offense; anything used, or designed to be used, in attacking an enemy, as a sword, a dagger, a club, a rifle, or a cannon.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ector faght in the fild felle of his Enmys.
Polexenas, a pert Duke, that the prinse met,

{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7740.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Before they durst
Embrace, they were by several servants search’d,

{{smaller block|The ''weapons'' of our warfare are not carnal. 2 Cor. x. 4.
<poem>All his mind is bent to holiness; . . .
His ''weapons'', holy saws of sacred writ.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., i. 3. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''3.''' In ''zoöl.'', any part or organ of the body which is or may be used as a means of attack or defense, as horns, hoofs, claws, spurs, stings, spines, teeth, electric organs, etc.; an arm or armature. ='''Syn. 1.''' See ''arm''<sup>2</sup>.}}

'''weapon†''' (wep′ọn), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''wepnien'', weapon, arm with weapons, < AS. ''wǣpnian'' = OFries. ''wēpna'' = OHG. ''wāfenen'' (cf. G. ''ge-waffnet'', ''bewaffnet'', armed with weapons) = Icel. ''vāpna'' = Sw. ''väpna'' = Dan. ''væbne'', arm; from the noun.]   To arm with weapons.

'''weaponed''' (wep′ọnd), ''a.''   [< ME. ''weppynd'', ''wæpned'', < AS. ''wǣpned'', pp. of ''wæpnian'', arm with weapons: see ''weapon'', ''v.'']   Armed for offense; furnished with offensive arms.
{{smaller block|<poem>Take xii of thi wyght ȝemen
Well ''weppynd'' be thei side.</poem>
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Monk'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 2).}}}}
{{smaller block|Be not afraid, though you do see me ''weapon’d.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 266.}}}}
{{smaller block|They . . . appointed three only, so ''weaponed'', to enter into the lists. {{right|''R. Peeke'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 636).}}}}

'''weaponless''' (wep′ọn-les), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wepenles'', < AS. ''wǣpenleas'' (= D. ''wapenloos'' = MLG. ''wapenlos'' = G. ''waffenlos'' = Icel. ''vāpnlauss'' = Sw. ''vapenlös'' = Dan. ''vaabenlös''), < ''wǣpen'', weapon, + ''-leas'' = E. ''-less''.]   Unarmed; having no weapon.
{{smaller block|Some High-way Theef, o’ my conscience, that forgets he is ''weaponless.'' {{right|''Brome'', Jovial Crew, iii.}}}}

'''weaponry†''' (wep′on-ri), ''n.''   [< ''weapon'' + ''-ry'' (see ''-ery'').]   Weapons in general. [Rare.]

'''weapon-salve†''' (wep′ọn-säv), ''n.'' A salve which was supposed to cure a wound by being applied to the weapon that made it. {{smaller|According to Sir Kenelm Digby, the salve produces sympathy between the wound and the weapon; he cites several instances to prove that “as the sword is treated the wound inflicted by it feels. Thus, if the instrument is kept wet, the wound will feel cool; if held to the fire, it will feel hot,” etc. This superstition is referred to in the following lines:}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She has ta’en the broken lance,
And washed it from the clotted gore,
And salved the splinter o’er and o’er.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iii. 23.}}}}

'''weapon-smith''' (wep′ọn-smith), ''n.'' One who makes weapons of war; an armorer. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It is unavoidable that the first mechanics — beyond the heroical ''weapon-smith'' on the one hand, and on the other the poor professors of such rude arts as the homestead cannot do without — . . . should be those who have no land.
{{right|''J. M. Kemble'', Saxons in England, ii. 7.}}}}

'''wear<sup>1</sup>''' (wãr), ''v.''; pret. ''wore'', pp. ''worn'', ppr. ''wearing''.   [< ME. ''weren'', ''werien'' (pret. ''werede'', pp. ''wered''), < AS. ''werian'' (pret. ''werode'', pp. ''werod''), wear, = OHG. ''werjan'', ''werjen'', clothe, = Icel. ''verja'', clothe, wrap, inclose, mount, also lay out, spend, = Goth. ''wasjan'' (pl. ''wasida''), clothe (the Goth. form showing interchange of ''r'' and ''s'': see ''rhotacism''), < √ ''was'', clothe, in L. ''vestis'', clothing, ''vestire'', clothe, Gr. ἐσθής, clothing: see ''vest''. The pret. ''wore'' (formerly also ''ware''), with the pp. ''worn'', is due to conformity with orig. strong preterits like ''bore'' < ''bear'', ''swore'' < ''swear'', ''tore'' < ''tear'', etc. (pp. ''born'', ''sworn'', ''torn'', etc.), the ME. pret. being weak, ''wered'', mod. E. *''weared''.]

'''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To carry or bear on the body as a covering or an appendage for warmth, decency, ornament, or other use; put or have on: as, to ''wear'' fine clothes; to ''wear'' diamonds.
{{smaller block|<poem>“I were nouȝt worthy, wote God,” quod Haukyn, “to ''were'' any clothes,
Ne noyther sherte ne shone saue for shame one,
To keure my caroigne.”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xiv. 331.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many ''wearing'' rapiers are afraid of goose-quills, and dare scarce come thither.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 2. 359.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thy Muse is a hagler, and ''weares'' cloathes vpon best-be-trust.
{{right|''Dekker'', Humorous Poet (Works, ed. Pearson, I. 245).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>On her head a caul of gold she ''ware.''</poem>
{{right|''A Praise of Mistress Ryce'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 38).}}}}
{{smaller block|From that time forth he [Canute] never would ''wear'' a Crown.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}
'''2.''' To use, affect, or be in the habit of using in one’s costume or adornment: as, to ''wear'' green.
{{smaller block|She ''wears'' her trains very long, as the great ladies do in Europe.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, vii.}}}}
'''3.''' To consume by frequent or habitual use; deteriorate or waste by wear; use up: as, boots well ''worn.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Continual Harvest ''wears'' the fruitful field.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love.}}}}
{{smaller block|But the object that most drew my attention, in the mysterious package, was a certain affair of fine red cloth, much ''worn'' and faded.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 34.}}}}
'''4.''' To waste or impair by rubbing or attrition; lessen or diminish by continuous action upon; consume; waste; destroy by degrees.
{{smaller block|<poem>When waterdrops have ''worn'' the stones of Troy,
And blind oblivion swallow’d cities up.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 2. 194.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The youth with broomy stumps began to trace
The kennel’s edge, where wheels had ''worn'' the place.</poem>
{{right|''Swift'', Description of Morning.}}}}
Hence—'''5.''' To exhaust; weary; fatigue.
{{smaller block|<poem>Since you have made the days and nights as one,
To ''wear'' your gentle limbs in my affairs.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, v. 1. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus were they plagued,
And ''worn'' with famine long.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 573.}}}}
'''6.''' To cause or produce by constant percussion or attrition; form by continual rubbing: as, a constant current of water will ''wear'' a channel in stone.
{{smaller block|Much attrition has ''worn'' every sentence into a bullet.
{{right|''Emerson'', English Traits, p. 118.}}}}
'''7.''' To efface; obliterate.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sort thy heart to patience;
These few days’ wonder will be quickly ''worn.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., ii. 4. 69.}}}}
'''8.''' To have or exhibit an appearance of; bear; carry; exhibit; show.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ne’er did poor steward ''wear'' a truer grief
For his undone lord than mine eyes for you.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iv. 3. 488.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I ''wore'' the Christian cause upon my sword,
Against his enemies.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Captain, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus both with Lamentations fill’d the Place,
’Till Sorrow seem’d to ''wear'' one common Face.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', Iliad.}}}}
{{smaller block|And my wife ''wears'' her benedictory look whenever she turns towards these young people.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, xxxii.}}}}
'''9.''' To disaccustom to one thing and accustom to another; bring gradually; lead: often with ''in'' or ''into'' before the new thing or state.
{{smaller block|Trials ''wear'' us ''into'' a liking of what possibly in the first essay displeased us.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}
{{smaller block|A man who has any relish for fine writing . . . receives stronger impressions from the masterly strokes of a great author every time he peruses him; besides that he naturally ''wears'' himself ''into'' the same manner of speaking and thinking.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 409.}}}}
'''10.''' ''Naut.'', to bring (a vessel) on another tack by turning her with her head away from the wind; veer. Also ''ware''.
{{smaller block|At three bells in the first watch the Death Ship had been ''wore'' to bring her starboard tacks aboard.
{{right|''W. C. Russell'', Death Ship, xxxii.}}}}
'''11†.''' To lay out; expend; spend; waste; squander. Compare ''ware''<sup>2</sup>.
{{smaller block|<poem>I saye thare leueings ar weill ''waird.''</poem>
{{right|''Lauder'', Dewtie of Kyngis (E. E. T. S.), l. 330.}}}}
{{smaller block|I haue ''wared'' all my mony in cowhides at Coleshill Market.
{{right|''Heywood'', 1 Edw. IV. (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, I. 43).}}}}
'''To wear away''', to impair, diminish, or destroy by gradual attrition or imperceptible action.
{{smaller block|Time and patience ''wear away'' pain and grief.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 531.}}}}
'''To wear off''', {{smaller|to remove or diminish by attrition or use: as, to ''wear off'' the stiffness of new shoes.}}—'''To wear one’s heart upon one’s sleeve.''' {{smaller|See ''heart''.}}—'''To wear out.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To wear till useless; render useless by wearing or using: as, to ''wear out'' a coat or a book. (''b'') To waste or destroy by degrees; consume tediously: as, to ''wear out'' life in idle projects.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
